newsitem.title: INDIA: India's rulers, Congress seek way out of impasse.
newsitem.headline: India's rulers, Congress seek way out of impasse.

text.p: India's ruling United Front coalition said on Tuesday that it would begin formal talks with the Congress party, raising hopes of a solution to the country's 10-day-old political crisis.
United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters that the coalition and Congress had agreed to begin formal talks on Wednesday morning.

"Informal talks between leaders of the United Front and Congress have yielded an understanding to the effect that formal talks between representatives of the Congress party and the United Front will start from (Wednesday) morning," Reddy said.
"Formal talks should be considered an advance," Reddy said.
Leaders of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition were expected to arrive in the Indian capital on Tuesday night, he said.
The ball was set rolling earlier in the day when Congress party chief Sitaram Kesri said he was willing to hold talks with Deve Gowda's minority coalition, which faces a vote of confidence on Friday.
"I am ready for talks if the proposal comes from their side. There is no doubt in it," Kesri told Reuters after addressing a rally in the Indian capital.
Kesri abruptly withdrew his party's support for Deve Gowda on March 30, triggering the political crisis which has jolted financial markets.
Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told a briefing: "So far no formal proposal has come."
But Reddy said: "Formal invitation is the only thing standing in the way for formal talks. That will go."

All-India Radio quoted Kesri as saying steps would be taken to ensure than India would not be forced into a mid-term poll, and a compromise between the ruling coalition and Congress appeared possible.
"We are hungry for respect, not for power," Kesri told party supporters at the rally.
"I don't have anything personal against Deve Gowda. When I speak, I speak of Deve Gowda as the prime minister," he added.
That marked a radical change in stance compared to a verbal attack launched by Kesri on Deve Gowda last week.

Kesri said the 10-month old minority United Front coalition, which has relied on the support of Congress's 138 deputies in parliament, never consulted the Congress party on important policy decisions.
Nor did the United Front support Congress in key state polls in Uttar Pradesh and Punjab, he said.
Earlier, another Congress leader, Sharad Pawar, said the party appreciated many aspects of the coalition's pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget, hailed by industry and businessmen.
The budget, now before parliament, has been held hostage by the political crisis.
But Pawar assured his audience at the rally that the Congress did not want to damage the economy.
"Congress does not want to trigger a financial crisis in the country," Pawar said.
The United Front coalition's highest decision-making body was to meet on Wednesday evening to discuss the crisis and seek ways to push the budget through parliament.
"The whole political crisis will get resolved by April 10," said a senior Congress leader who asked not to be identified.
